name: Cacao use at Santa Ana-La Florida, upper Amazon
summary: Cacao residues at Santa Ana-La Florida in southeast Ecuador document use about 5,300 years ago, including cacao in funerary vessel contexts.
description: Starch grains, theobromine residues and ancient DNA on artifacts attest to cacao use at Santa Ana-La Florida in southeast Ecuador. The excavation report describes cacao starch recovered from ceramic bottles associated with funerary offerings. The form of the drink and the manner in which the plant was obtained remain uncertain.

impact.note: One society in one region used it (reach 1); a new food and drink plant added to an existing diet (depth 1); later cacao use elsewhere may descend from upper Amazon use, but no source here ties it to this community, so generativity stays at 1.

date.label: c. 3350 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Cacao use at Santa Ana-La Florida, Ecuador, is dated to about 5,300 years ago, which is about 3350 BCE by the 1950 convention.

evidence.supports: dating from approximately 5,300 years ago recovered from the Santa Ana-La Florida (SALF) site in southeast Ecuador
Reports cacao starch in ceramic bottles and cacao markers across ceramic and stone vessels, including funerary contexts.

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Coordinates of Santa Ana-La Florida: the place is given as the town of Palanda, the canton centre near the site, because no fetched source gave site coordinates.
Whether the upper Amazon people domesticated cacao or only gathered wild pods; the genomic domestication signal in Central America dates to about 3,600 years ago.
How and when cacao reached Mesoamerica, and whether Mesoamerican chocolate needs its own derived record.

Later analyses report cacao in regional ceramic assemblages assigned to phases that overlap or begin before the Santa Ana-La Florida date. Directly dated specimen contexts and finer genetic comparisons would help resolve priority and regional movement.

evidence.supports: Sampled San Jacinto and Valdivia items are assigned to broad cultural intervals. The study reports multiple genetic affinities in coastal assemblages.

research.note: The 2018 study gives several independent analytical proxies within the same site assemblage. The excavator’s earlier report supplies vessel context. Relative priority among contemporary or earlier reported occurrences requires sample-level dating.
